summary:
Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which applies in full. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia covering sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the position a visitor actually encounters: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is active and measurable. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel. It states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and it carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. It affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

No deviation from the national position material enough to score separately was identified for this autonomous okrug (±0.02), and the division is therefore assessed at the national score. For a trans traveller that position means same-sex marriage is banned, gender transition is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, with enforcement risk active rather than theoretical.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement wave is national in scope, so the risk a visitor faces in Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra mirrors what is documented in the federal cities. The Guardian's account of the Moscow bar raids of 17 January 2024 and The Moscow Times' summary of 2025 both describe a pattern of raids, arrests and extremism charges rather than isolated incidents, and the eighteenfold growth in propaganda-law cases reported by Meduza indicates rising volume as well as rising severity.

Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office position that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention gives that call a formal procedural route in one destination country. The US Level 4 advisory places Russia among the small number of states carrying a blanket Do Not Travel instruction, with LGBT-specific warnings attached to it.

Adjacent risks extend beyond prosecution. The Associated Press report of a man dying in a pretrial detention facility after extremism-related charges, and the BBC Russian account of nine months of forced confinement in a conversion-therapy centre, indicate that detention and private coercion can both produce lethal or physically coercive outcomes for people caught up in these laws.

outOfScopeNotes:

The regional assessment rests on the national framework and national enforcement data, and whether local authorities in the okrug have issued their own directives or conducted their own operations is not sourced here.
